summary: Documents security concerns with IP tunnels and proposes strategies for mitigating them, to raise awareness among administrators and protocol developers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: An IP tunnel carries one packet inside another, which can let traffic cross a firewall or NAT without the usual checks on the inner packet. RFC 6169 describes the resulting security concerns and ways administrators and protocol designers can reduce them.

questions: what security risks do ip tunnels create
how can tunnels bypass firewall inspection
subtitle: Security risks and mitigations for IP packets carried through tunnels over UDP or TCP.

tldr.problem: Tunnels can carry inner IP traffic through NATs and firewalls without applying the network's usual inspection and filtering to that traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys tunnel-related risks, including bypassed filtering, harder packet inspection, longer-lived NAT mappings, guessable addresses, and unauthenticated tunnel-server changes.
tldr.outcome: The document offers operational and protocol-design mitigations, such as limiting tunnel use, protecting tunnel interfaces, and authenticating the tunnel server.

today: RFC 6169 is Informational and was published in April 2011. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: How Tunnels Can Bypass Network Controls
sections.content:
Tunnel protocols can carry IP packets over UDP or TCP to cross NATs and firewalls. A network security device that does not understand the tunnel may inspect only the outer headers, leaving the inner packet outside its usual policy checks.

The same issue affects ingress and egress filtering: the network carrying the tunnel cannot check the inner source and destination addresses unless it understands the tunnel. The RFC also warns that a tunneled packet with source-routing information may cause a tunnel client to forward it to an unexpected next hop.
sections.plainLanguage: A firewall that sees only the outer packet may not inspect or filter the IP packet inside it. Tunnel endpoints need to apply appropriate controls to that inner traffic.

sections.title: Why Tunnel Inspection Is Difficult
sections.content:
Some tunnels use well-known ports or protocol numbers, but others use changing ports or share ports with ordinary traffic. Blocking a tunnel's setup port may stop new tunnels without affecting existing ones. Filtering every possible tunnel requires examining a large range of traffic.

Deep inspection may require parsing packets on a device's slower processing path and can reduce throughput. The RFC says inspecting tunneled traffic is complex and often impractical; if a network must monitor IP traffic, it recommends avoiding tunnels across the security boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tunnels are easy to identify, but others resemble ordinary traffic. Examining every packet for a tunnel can be costly and may not be practical.

sections.title: NAT Mappings and Exposure
sections.content:
An active tunnel can keep a mapped port open on a NAT device so remote hosts can send packets to the tunnel client. Those packets pass through outer-IP, UDP or TCP, tunnel, and inner-IP processing. Each step adds exposed processing before an inner firewall can filter the packet.

The mapping may stay open and stable longer than an ordinary NAT mapping, making it easier to discover. Some public tunnels also allow inbound connectivity from the Internet and can reduce the NAT's usual source filtering. The RFC recommends minimizing tunnel use, deactivating tunnels when no longer needed, and using a host firewall on the tunnel interface.
sections.plainLanguage: An active tunnel can keep a NAT mapping available for incoming traffic. Limiting how long a tunnel runs and filtering its interface can reduce this exposure.

sections.title: Tunnel Addresses and Host Information
sections.content:
Some tunnel protocols use structured or predictable address ranges. This can make tunnel endpoints easier to find than ordinary IPv6 addresses. An address associated with a tunnel may also reveal which client software or platform is likely in use.

The RFC recommends that tunnel designers avoid easily guessed addresses and use random values in otherwise unused fields to add uncertainty. It also discusses randomizing tunnel server settings or client ports to reduce some forms of profiling.
sections.plainLanguage: A structured tunnel address can make a host easier to locate and identify. Random values and less predictable server settings can reduce some of that information.

sections.title: Authenticating and Managing Tunnel Endpoints
sections.content:
If an attacker can change a tunnel client's server setting or redirect its server-name lookup, an unauthenticated tunnel may place the attacker between the client and its destination. The attacker could observe traffic or, in some cases, impersonate a remote peer.

The RFC recommends authenticating the tunnel server or the method used to determine its address. It also recommends controlling who can change tunnel settings, making the current setting easy to inspect, preferring native connectivity when available, and using on-premises tunnel servers where appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: A client should verify the identity of its tunnel server before sending traffic through it. Administrators should be able to control and inspect tunnel settings.
